nameStory: The name 'hairy tare' comes from the plant's fuzzy stems and leaves, covered in soft hairs that you can feel when you brush against them. 'Tare' is an old agricultural term for weedy plants that grow among grain crops - farmers considered these plants worthless 'tares' that had to be separated from valuable wheat and barley.
description: Hairy tare is a delicate climbing vine in the pea family that scrambles over other plants using tiny tendrils. This slender annual grows up to 2 feet long, with soft, feathery compound leaves and tiny white or pale pink flowers that look like miniature pea blossoms. Its fuzzy stems and leaves give it a distinctly soft, almost velvety texture that sets it apart from other vetches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or very pale pink pea-like flowers, only about 1/8 inch long, growing in clusters of 1-8 on slender stalks - much smaller than other vetches

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 6-16 small, narrow leaflets that feel soft and fuzzy to touch, ending in branched tendrils that help the plant climb

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Delicate climbing vine that scrambles weakly over grasses and low plants, with thin stems covered in soft white hairs

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hairy seed pods about 1/4 inch long containing just 2 tiny seeds, much smaller than other vetch pods

habitat: Look for hairy tare in disturbed soils, field edges, roadsides, and waste areas throughout New England. It prefers sandy or well-drained soils and often grows mixed in with grasses and other weedy plants in open, sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin growing with their characteristic fuzzy leaves and climbing habit.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from June through August with tiny white flowers, followed by small hairy seed pods that ripen quickly.
seasonality.fall: Plants die back after setting seed, leaving dried stems and empty pods that may persist briefly.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant is completely absent - only seeds remain dormant in the soil until next spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'hairy vetch' sometimes, hairy tare produces the tiniest flowers of any vetch in New England - they're so small you might need a magnifying glass to see their pea-flower shape clearly!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other vetches, but hairy tare's flowers are dramatically smaller than any other vetch species. Memory trick: 'Hairy tare has tiny flowers to spare' - if the pea-like flowers are bigger than your pinky nail, it's probably a different vetch.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name was recently changed from Vicia hirsuta to Ervilia hirsuta by some botanists, so you might see both names in field guides. This reflects ongoing research into vetch relationships, but most resources still use the Vicia name.
compareHints: Hairy tare stands out from its vetch relatives primarily by size - everything about it is smaller and more delicate. While tufted vetch and hairy vetch have showy purple flower clusters and common vetch has larger pink or purple blooms, hairy tare's flowers are tiny and white. Its soft, fuzzy texture is also more pronounced than the hairiness found on hairy vetch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted vetch stands out from its vetch relatives by having the most densely packed, one-sided flower clusters that hang downward like purple bunches of grapes.

Among the vetches in New England, hairy vetch stands out for its distinctly fuzzy stems - tufted vetch has smooth stems, common vetch has larger individual flowers, and the smaller vetches like hairy tare have much tinier flowers and leaflets.
Common vetch stands out from its relatives by having flowers that appear singly or in pairs rather than in clusters like tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
Among New England vetches, lentil vetch is the smallest and most delicate, with the tiniest flowers and smoothest texture.

Among New England's vetches, bush vetch stands out for its short flower clusters of just 2-6 blooms, while tufted vetch has long, showy spikes of many flowers and hairy vetch has dense, cone-shaped clusters.
Among the vetch family in New England, large yellow vetch is unmistakable due to its bright yellow flowers - all other local vetches have purple, pink, or white blooms.
Among New England's vetches, spring vetch stands out for its diminutive size - both the flowers and overall plant are much smaller than tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
Unlike other vetches in New England, fava beans are much larger, bushier plants that don't climb or sprawl.
